Issued at 1141 PM MDT Mon Sep 21 2026

The threat for higher-end flooding is increasing, especially for 
south-central New Mexico. The overall forecast pattern and is more
or less locked in, now it is down to specific details like which
specific arroyo and stream basins see the most rainfall. 

Our upper level low over California is slowly weakening as it
drifts into Nevada, while 200 mb streamline analysis shows broad
upper level diffluence over the Sierra Madres near the junction 
of Sonora, Chihuahua, and Sinaloa. Convection in this region was 
fairly concentrated this evening, but water vapor imagery shows 
some signs of a tight upper level low taking shape, as expected. 
This system will weaken into a shortwave trough as it rolls 
northwards up the Sierra Madres Tuesday, aided by broadening upper
level diffluence across Chihuahua and New Mexico and a 
strengthening subtropical jet streak in SE Arizona.

Meanwhile, at the surface, the back door cold front has topped the
Sacramento and Guadalupe Mountains. Mesonet obs show steady east
winds with a few gusts around 20-25 mph in parts of Alamogordo,
and the upper range of WSMR. The Dell City West Texas Mesonet 
station also has an east wind along with PX Well RAWS. Expect some
low stratus and fog to develop along the east slopes of the 
Sacramentos as cooler/moisture air seeps in closer to dawn, 
lagging behind the initial wind shift. A few spots could see brief
dense fog.

By Sunrise, some sparse showers may be on-going in SW New
Mexico, and the back door front tries to reach the Arizona state 
line by mid-morning. Thunderstorms look to initiate tomorrow 
afternoon along the higher terrain, but also near the cold front 
in SW New Mexico. Outflow looks to push the front back to the east
a bit, falling in line with a surface and low level trough that 
develops ahead of the approaching shortwave trough from the south.
By evening, the surface front and low level trough will become 
the focus for intense moisture convergence. This is where the 
heaviest rain will focus, with several waves of showers and 
embedded thunderstorms training across the broader region. 
Unfortunately, there is still some uncertainty into where exactly 
this region sets up. Notably, a few high res models have a sharp 
eastern cutoff to the significant precip Tuesday night, with some 
producing 2-3 inches of rain in parts of south-central New Mexico,
and scant amounts over El Paso. 

The most likely scenario broadly produces 2-3 inches of rain
from the east slopes of the Black Range to the San Andres
Mountain, and south across much of Luna and Dona Ana County,
tapering off into western El Paso County. The worst-case scenario
type model runs (e.g., the 00Z HRRR with its hopefully-outlier
cataclysmic totals east of the Black Range, appear to the result
of repeated training of the max precip rates over the same area
with very little variation. The more likely scenario would see
isolated pockets of 3 to 5 inches within the broader 2-3 inch
area.

That said, the greatest probabilities when looking at various
exceedance levels (1 inch, 2 inch, 3 inch) focus on western 
Sierra County and northern Dona Ana County. All the long-run 
arroyos coming off the Black Range towards the Rio Grande are at 
risk of seeing higher-end flooding. This same area has broadly 
seen 2-3 inches of rain over the past 7 days, including portions 
of the Black Range crest, but mainly east of the Lake 
Valley/Highway 27 corridor all the way into the northern end of 
the Jornada del Muerto. That extra saturation will enhance runoff.


A fair amount of the heavier rain will likely fall into basins
that feed in south of Caballo Dam (everything south of Percha
Creek), which will likely bring significant rises in the Rio
Grande. Thankfully, water levels have dried back up through most
of the Rio Grande south of Caballo, but we may still come close to
bankfull in the reaches from Percha Dam south through Selden
Canyon, down to around Leasburg. 

Heavy rainfall is likely to be ongoing Wednesday morning,
impacting the morning commute, especially if El Paso ends up back
in the heaviest rain axis. The shortwave trough will move north
into the Gila region by midday Wednesday, with a trailing vort
lobe curling down towards El Paso and west of the Big Bend. The
heaviest rain will lift northeast as it does so, with the
intensity moderating a bit. Much of southwestern New Mexico could
see a significant dry period Wednesday afternoon. Meanwhile, the
focus for rain will shift east.

The trough will linger over Hudspeth County heading into Wednesday
Night and Thursday, but the overall QPF amounts look to pale in
comparison to what central areas are looking to get Tue Night/Wed
AM. Kept the Flood Watch as is, though the eastern extension of it
looks questionable.
